name: Erik Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What do you make at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 58, and I run the seamer that fixes lids onto aluminium drink cans. My vocational machine-operations certificate got me onto the floor, and eleven years here have made me decent at spotting a bad seam on the cut-open sample. I can reset the feed and document faults; a fitter handles motor repairs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do your household and new tools fit with the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nadia works in a school library, and our grown son and daughter have their own homes. Weekend shifts give me above-usual operator pay, we have around a year's expenses saved, and plenty of nearby drink plants advertise machine jobs. I use AI every day to search manuals and organise seam measurements, then check the cut-open can and approved tolerance sheet. I'm happy to test new controls early on a safe line. I also want union rules so night and weekend operators get paid access to any training. Retirement is close enough to discuss, but we haven't checked a written income against our living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the seamer crew that quicker sales forecasts could prevent a shortage of lids. I would still cut open a can at the start of the run and measure its seam before the pallets move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher weekend rate, Nadia's wages and a year's reserve cover our bills. AI in the office does not alter the seam itself, so I would not expect this version to take my machine shift. The screen could make the supplies steadier, which is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep testing cut-open seams and use my existing daily AI manual searches to organise measurement notes, checking each number against the approved sheet. I would put a fresh amount from each full paid weekend month into savings after household costs. At the next union shift meeting I would ask whether any new delivery target changes our staffed inspection time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A forecast is useful if the can lid still stays sealed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the cut-open sample show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see whether the two layers of metal have hooked together evenly and measure the overlap. A bad overlap means I stop and reset the seamer before another pallet is filled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask about inspection time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rushed output target can make people skip samples. At the union meeting I want a written interval for cut-open checks, not just a new pallet number.

The union should protect **sample time** when output targets change.
think: The **weekend premium** and one-year reserve cover current bills.
Office AI does not yet change my **physical seamer shift**.
do: **Keep** cutting sample cans and verifying seam overlap.
**Save** new full-month weekend wages after household costs.
**Ask** at the union meeting for written seam-sample time.
feel: **Calm** because the current paid seamer work remains needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues an AI stock plan may arrive before robots can load a seamer. I would try a guarded seam camera on scrap cans if the factory pays for the test and shows us the proposed roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like learning early, but a camera could let the plant combine weekend runs and take away part of my premium. Our savings and Nadia's wage buy time, yet a lower regular rate would change our plans for stopping work. Daily manual searches do not teach a new camera control by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the proposed weekend roster and a paid guarded camera trial. If offered, I would learn the AI seam-alert screen on good and deliberately faulty scrap cans, comparing each alert with a cut-open sample and the approved tolerance sheet beside the fitter. If my paid weekend hours actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe nearby seamer jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and shift pattern covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of premium hours, though I want the trial. A clever camera should earn trust one cut-open can at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault would you deliberately make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter could set a scrap batch with too little seam overlap, then restore the approved setting. I would compare the alert with a cut-open measurement, under a guard with no hands near a running head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not take any nearby job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advertised weekend bonus may be different from guaranteed base pay. I would need the posting, actual shift hours and journey cost before leaving this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch AGI could plan can orders in 2028, while capable robots to feed and inspect cans arrive around 2031. We should bargain for paid qualification places and real retained jobs before the seamer line changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can do that physical work. I expect a lot of manual seamer shifts to go, perhaps mine; our year's reserve and nearby factories give us options, but similar plants may automate too. Losing my higher weekend rate would be a serious income change, even if we could cover the first months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend the scheduled union bargaining meeting to seek written staffing dates and funded practical places. I would enrol in a locally accepted can-quality certificate only if fees, paid release and supervised guarded seamer practice are offered. After passing, if my hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shift hours covers our bills; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe seamer jobs on those same terms and keep any paid shifts in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than helpless. We have a cushion and plenty of plants to ask, but I would not pretend the weekend rate follows me automatically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What practical work would the course need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut open a bad seam, measure the overlap and isolate the seamer before adjusting a feed. A trainer must watch on a guarded line, rather than sign off a screen exercise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income, Nadia's reliable pay and our costs add up after housing and health expenses. We have not verified that, so I would apply for real paid work first.

Our union should negotiate **paid qualification places** before the line changes.

**Apply** after cuts to posted safe quality if qualified, or seamer fallback, at viable net pay.

fieldNote: He sees **2031 physical robots** as the wage risk after 2028 AGI first changes order planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI might plan drink orders in 2031 and capable robots might reach the seamer around 2034. Five years is enough to test an accepted course and compare real nearby job offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. Nadia and I might decide to stop before then if written retirement income covers costs, but that is not settled. The year saved and the current weekend premium let me try a practical route without betting the rent on a course title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add new premium wages to savings after full paid months and household bills, then check which can-quality certificate nearby plants actually list. If an accepted funded course with paid release and supervised guarded practice opens, I would enrol. After qualifying, if hours fall, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs whose guaranteed wages after travel and shifts cover bills; if no place opens, I would apply to posted safe seamer roles on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about replacing the premium, but I have time to compare evidence. A year saved gives me room to be selective about a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you verify the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its exact credential to current local quality postings and ask two plants whether its seamer practice counts. If neither accepts it, I would keep looking for a funded place they do accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you truly stop before 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income, Nadia's pay and our reserves reliably meet housing, food and health costs. If that arithmetic works, I would leave before a robot forces the issue; otherwise I would keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan drink orders in 2036 and capable robots could reach the seamer around 2039. Ten years lets us decide from written household figures whether I need to work that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those robots handle the line, if I am still employed. Our higher current pay, Nadia's work and a year's reserve keep near-term bills safe. I hope to stop before 2039, but only if actual retirement income covers housing, food and health costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid seamer shifts and request written retirement-income estimates with a full cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would enrol in a locally accepted can-quality course only when funding, paid release and guarded supervised practice are offered. If I remain at work after 2036 and paid hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local seamer or quality jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and shifts meets our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant choice, but secure on this year's income. I would rather measure what stopping costs than let a machine decide the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia and I would compare written income with rent, food, travel and likely health expenses. If those figures reliably cover us, I would stop before the robot line arrives; if not, I would keep earning or apply for real jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not give up a secure wage for an unrecognised badge. If a nearby employer accepts it and the plant funds paid guarded practice, I would consider the offered course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture would test us most, because my seamer weekend rate could go before retirement income is clear. A funded guarded quality place that nearby plants accept, real posted jobs at enough pay after travel, and a negotiated staffing timetable would help. I would keep the paid shift until a genuine route opens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a robot can explain a bad seam to the person buying the drink. A can that leaks in a customer's hand is still our factory's responsibility.

headlineQuote: A can that leaks in a customer's hand is still our factory's responsibility.
portrait: **Erik**, 58, is an experienced mid-level drink-can seamer operator with a vocational certificate and average machine skill.
He and his **partner Nadia** have grown children, higher weekend pay, about a year's expenses saved and plenty of nearby drink plants.
He uses **AI daily** for manuals and notes, checks physical seams and supports union access to paid safe practical training.
Possible **2031 physical robots** threaten premium shifts; an earlier stop depends on written retirement income covering real costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 seamer robots** could remove his higher paid weekend shifts before retirement income or replacement wages are verified.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **accepted funded guarded training**, posted local jobs with viable net pay and a negotiated written staffing timetable.
